title: She Led 11-9 at the Interval. Then Yamaguchi Scored Six Straight and Sindhu's Title Drought Hit 18 Months.
excerpt: PV Sindhu's semifinal loss at the Australian Open means India's best shuttler is still searching for a 2026 breakthrough ahead of the Asian Games in Nagoya.
body:
PV Sindhu was doing everything right. She was ahead at the mid-game interval, controlling the rallies, dictating the tempo. Then Akane Yamaguchi scored six consecutive points, and the story of Sindhu's 2026 season wrote itself again: close, but not quite close enough.

The former world champion lost 22-20, 21-12 to the reigning world champion and world No. 3 Yamaguchi in the women's singles semifinal of the Australian Open in Sydney on Saturday, ending India's campaign in the BWF Super 500 tournament.

It was Sindhu's second semifinal of the 2026 BWF World Tour season — the first came at the Malaysia Open in January — and the result extended a title drought that now stretches back 18 months to the Syed Modi International in December 2024.

## A First Game That Deserved Better

The opening game was everything a rivalry between two seasoned champions should be. Sindhu, seeded third in Sydney, came out aggressive, building a slender lead and carrying a 11-9 advantage into the interval.

But Yamaguchi, the three-time world champion who has spent the past year rebuilding her own game after a dip in form, responded with a devastating burst. Six straight points swung the momentum decisively, and despite Sindhu clawing her way back to save one game point at 20-19, the Japanese shuttler held her nerve to take it 22-20.

The second game was a different contest entirely. Yamaguchi reeled off seven unanswered points to build an unassailable lead, and from there the match became a procession. The 21-12 scoreline was ruthless — and it was complete in just 43 minutes.

## The Rivalry Tilts

The defeat was the 29th career meeting between the two veterans, and it shifted the head-to-head record to 15-14 in Sindhu's favour. But the trend tells a sharper story: Yamaguchi has now won four of their last five encounters, with Sindhu's only recent victory coming via a mid-match retirement by the Japanese at the Malaysia Open.

At 30, Sindhu remains India's most decorated badminton player — an Olympic gold and silver medallist, a world champion, and a figure whose star power extends far beyond the court. But the gap between her best form and the consistency needed to win titles has widened, and the 2026 season has offered more questions than answers.

## Asian Games and the Road Ahead

There is, however, a clear path forward. Sindhu was named in India's squad for the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya alongside men's doubles stars Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, giving her a major multi-sport target for September.

Before that, the Women's World Tour continues through the summer, and Sindhu will be looking to convert semifinal appearances into something more — starting, perhaps, with recognizing that the first game in Sydney proved she can still compete with the best in the world. The second game proved that competing is not the same as winning.

For NRI fans who grew up watching Sindhu duel with Carolina Marín and Nozomi Okuhara on the biggest stages, the Australian Open was a familiar cocktail of hope and heartbreak. The talent is still there. The breakthrough just keeps slipping away.
